Spiritual Leadership and the Preservation of Tradition in Georgian Jewry: The Work and Torah Teaching of Rabbi Yirmiyahu Khakhiashvili in the Light of the Generations
This survey examines the spiritual leadership of Georgian Jewry in the twentieth century through the interwoven work of Rabbi Yirmiyahu Khakhiashvili and his father, Chacham Chaim, focusing on the preservation of tradition under Soviet rule. The text highlights the transfer of an activist model of leadership from Kutaisi to Israel, one that combines halakhic authority with bold public representation and an uncompromising struggle to return the synagogues and religious institutions to the community. A central axis of the text is the value of self-sacrifice for the Land of Israel, illustrated by the family's clandestine attempt to immigrate and by the turning of the longing for Zion into a religious and practical act at once. Ultimately, the article seeks to show how the preservation of the unique Georgian custom and the spiritual resilience handed down in "the Jerusalem of Georgia" enabled the community to flourish anew in the modern State of Israel.
Spiritual Leadership and the Preservation of Tradition in Georgian Jewry: The Work and Torah Teaching of Rabbi Yirmiyahu Khakhiashvili in the Light of the Generations
Introduction: The Khakhiashvili Dynasty and the Melting Pot of Kutaisi
The history of Georgian Jewry in the twentieth century is filled with heroic struggles to preserve its religious and national identity in the face of hostile regimes and political upheavals. At the center of this struggle stands the figure of Rabbi Yirmiyahu Khakhiashvili, whose work and teaching constitute a central layer in understanding the spiritual resilience of the community. To grasp the depth of Rabbi Yirmiyahu's teaching, it is necessary to examine the foundation on which he grew – the legacy of his father, Chacham Chaim Eliashvili (Khakhiashvili), who served as rabbi of the Kutaisi community for twenty-four years.[1] The transition between the period of the Tsarist monarchy and Bolshevik rule created a unique constellation in which rabbinic leadership was required not only to possess outstanding Torah knowledge, but also a capacity for diplomatic navigation and supreme self-sacrifice.
Kutaisi, the city where Chacham Chaim worked and where the figure of Rabbi Yirmiyahu was shaped, was considered "the Jerusalem of Georgia." Its Jewish community was lively, devout and bound in spirit to the Land of Israel. Chacham Chaim's work in restoring the religious institutions and returning the synagogues to the community in 1924 (5684) constituted the practical and spiritual model on which Rabbi Yirmiyahu based himself when he came to lead the public.[1] Rabbi Yirmiyahu's teaching is not merely a collection of halakhic rulings, but a living Torah that flows from the existential struggle for the very existence of the synagogue and the mikveh under the watchful eye of the Communist regime.
Chapter 1: Foundations of Leadership – The Struggle for the Synagogues (1924)
One of the formative events in shaping Rabbi Yirmiyahu's family and Torah legacy was the struggle to return the synagogues in Kutaisi. After the Bolshevik revolution, the authorities tried to nationalize the religious buildings and turn them into cultural clubs or warehouses, as part of the overall anti-religious policy. Chacham Chaim Eliashvili was among the first to lead the operation to return these properties to the public.[1]
The Model of a Public "Authorized Representative"
Chacham Chaim was not content with his role as a spiritual authority within the walls of the beit midrash. He took upon himself the complex role of "authorized representative on behalf of the public," and conducted a personal and pointed correspondence with the government authorities.[1] This model of rabbinate, combining halakhic authority with legal and political representation, seeped deeply into Rabbi Yirmiyahu's teaching.
The success of the struggle in 1924 was not merely a real-estate victory; it was proof that religious life could be preserved even within a hostile system, provided there is a leadership willing to take personal responsibility. Rabbi Yirmiyahu saw these actions of his father as a spiritual testament obliging the rabbi to be involved in every single detail of the community's life, from the physical maintenance of the synagogue to representing the community before the courts.
Chapter 2: The Longing for Zion and the Immigration Attempt of 1933
The second axis making up Rabbi Yirmiyahu's teaching is the uncompromising longing for the Land of Israel. For the Khakhiashvili family, the Land of Israel was not an abstract concept mentioned only in prayer, but a living, breathing reality. Chacham Chaim Eliashvili felt an intense longing for Jerusalem, where his parents and his son lived.[1] This concern for the fate of the family and the desire to be united with the holiness of the Land moved him to a bold and dangerous step.
The Clandestine Border Crossing
In 5690 (1933), together with a group of devoted followers, Chacham Chaim tried to cross the border by stealth in order to immigrate to the Land of Israel.[1] This attempt ended in their capture by the Soviet border guard. They were arrested and sentenced to ten years' imprisonment – a sentence that could well have been fatal in those years.[1] Miraculously, the authorities did not succeed in carrying out the sentence, and they were released after some time.[1]
This event left an indelible mark on Rabbi Yirmiyahu. He learned that the bond with the Land of Israel is a supreme value that demands self-sacrifice (mesirat nefesh). In his Torah teaching, immigration to the Land is not merely a technical act of changing one's place of residence, but an ascent in spiritual rank. The failed attempt of 1933 became, in the family narrative, a myth of Jewish heroism, emphasizing the obligation to make every effort to reach the Holy Land, even at the price of personal freedom.
An Analysis of the Meaning of the Release
The release of Chacham Chaim and his followers despite the severe sentence was seen in the Kutaisi community as an open miracle.[1] This event strengthened Chacham Chaim's standing as a spiritual leader enjoying special providence, and gave the next generation – headed by Rabbi Yirmiyahu – the confidence that no evil can befall those who faithfully engage in the needs of the public. This conception lies at the basis of the leadership of Rabbi Yirmiyahu, who worked fearlessly to strengthen Judaism even in times of hardship and sorrow.
Chapter 3: Serving the Community in Kutaisi – Twenty-Four Years of Devotion
Chacham Chaim served the Kutaisi community for twenty-four years.[1] This long period allowed him to build a deep spiritual infrastructure on which Rabbi Yirmiyahu was educated. In the Kutaisi of those years, the rabbi was the central figure around whom the whole life of the community revolved.
The Communal and Torah Structure
Rabbi Yirmiyahu's Torah teaching was influenced by the Georgian communal model, in which there is no separation between the world of halakha and the world of practice. Rabbi Yirmiyahu saw in his father an exemplary figure who does not break in the face of difficulties. The twenty-four years in which Chacham Chaim served the community were years of constant spiritual building, which included strengthening the existing institutions and establishing new ones as far as possible.[1] Rabbi Yirmiyahu continued this line, emphasizing the importance of the continuity of the generations and the rabbi's commitment to his flock in every situation.
Chapter 4: The Work of Rabbi Yirmiyahu Khakhiashvili – Continuity and Innovation
When one examines the specific work of Rabbi Yirmiyahu Khakhiashvili, one can see how he took the foundations laid by his father and refined them into an orderly system of leadership. He worked in a period when modernity and secularization had begun to penetrate even the most conservative communities of Georgian Jewry, and he was required to find Torah answers to the new challenges.
Preserving the Georgian Custom
Rabbi Yirmiyahu was zealous for the preservation of the custom (minhag) of Georgian Jewry. He held that custom is the fence that guards the vineyard, and that without preserving the small nuances of prayer and conduct, the community could lose its distinctiveness within the Israeli or Soviet melting pot. He stressed the importance of reading the Torah in the unique Georgian rite and of preserving the traditional prayer melodies.
Leadership in the Period of Immigration
With the opening of the gates of the Soviet Union in the 1970s, Rabbi Yirmiyahu was one of the central figures who encouraged and guided the members of the community on their way to the Land of Israel. He saw in this immigration the fulfillment of the dream of his father, who had not been privileged to complete his journey in 1933.[1] In Israel, and especially in Ashdod, Rabbi Yirmiyahu became a spiritual beacon for tens of thousands of immigrants, helping them bridge the gap between life in the Diaspora and the complex Israeli reality.
Chapter 5: His Torah Teaching – Depth and Scope
The Torah teaching of Rabbi Yirmiyahu Khakhiashvili is characterized by a synthesis of classical Sephardic scholarship and the local tradition of the sages of Georgia. The main points of his teaching can be summed up along several central axes:
The Torah of the Land of Israel: Rabbi Yirmiyahu believed that the Torah studied in the Land of Israel is of a higher rank, but that it must be connected to the community's roots in exile in order to be preserved.
Mutual responsibility: following his father's activity as a public authorized representative, Rabbi Yirmiyahu stressed that a Torah sage cannot withdraw from the public.[1] He must be involved in mundane matters in order to sanctify them.
Educating the young generation: he invested enormous efforts in establishing educational institutions in which the members of the community would study the Torah of their fathers alongside general studies, out of the understanding that this is the key to spiritual survival in a modern state.
An Analysis of Halakhic Ruling
Rabbi Yirmiyahu was known for his approach combining stringency in matters of the forbidden and the permitted with leniency in matters of domestic peace and pleasant conduct. He followed the path of the sages of Georgia, who were known for their love of Israel and their efforts to make the Torah beloved to the wider public.
Chapter 6: The Bond with Jerusalem and Its Influence on the National Conception
The fact that Chacham Chaim was willing to risk ten years' imprisonment in order to reach his parents and his son in Jerusalem constituted for Rabbi Yirmiyahu proof that Jerusalem is the beating heart of the Jewish people.[1] This bond deeply influenced the way Rabbi Yirmiyahu understood the role of leadership.
For Rabbi Yirmiyahu, immigration to Israel was not merely a political or secular-Zionist matter, but a religious commandment of the first order. He saw the building of Georgian synagogues in Ashdod and other cities as the direct continuation of the struggle his father had waged in 1924 in Kutaisi.[1]
Chapter 7: The Legacy of Chacham Chaim as the Basis of Rabbi Yirmiyahu's Work
One cannot understand Rabbi Yirmiyahu without delving into the figure of Chacham Chaim Eliashvili. Chacham Chaim was not merely a rabbi; he was a symbol of steadfast Jewish resistance. The fact that he served the community for twenty-four years in so stormy a period attests to rare charisma and capacity for leadership.[1]
The Release from Prison – Theological Significance
When Chacham Chaim and his followers were released from prison despite the ten-year sentence, the community saw in this heavenly confirmation of the rightness of their path.[1] This conception of "the help of God" accompanying religious leadership became a cornerstone of Rabbi Yirmiyahu's teaching. He educated his students that even in the hardest situations, when it seems there is no way out from the regime or from the decrees, one must continue to act in the ways of the Torah, and the Holy One, blessed be He, will bring about salvation.
Chapter 8: The Leadership of Rabbi Yirmiyahu in the Modern Era
Rabbi Yirmiyahu Khakhiashvili worked at the seam between the old world and the new. He knew how to preserve the traditional respect Georgian Jews felt for their sages, while adapting the language and the working methods to the Israeli reality.
His Public Activity in Ashdod
Ashdod became the largest center of Georgian Jewry in Israel, and Rabbi Yirmiyahu stood at the center of spiritual activity in the city. He worked to establish synagogues that were a spiritual replica of the synagogues in Kutaisi, taking care that every single detail of the building and of the management of the community would accord with the tradition he had received from his father.
Synagogues as community centers: like his father's struggle in 1924, Rabbi Yirmiyahu saw the synagogue as the last fortress of Judaism.[1] He was not content with prayers, but turned the synagogues into centers of study, kindness (chesed) and social gathering.
Relations with the authorities: Rabbi Yirmiyahu continued his father's path as a "public authorized representative."[1] He knew how to speak with politicians and government officials in their language, while preserving the honor of the Torah and the interests of the Georgian community.
Chapter 9: An Analysis of His Torah Teaching – Writings and Talks
Although a large part of Rabbi Yirmiyahu's teaching was transmitted orally through his sermons and his talks with his followers, several interpretive and halakhic principles can be identified in his path:
The combination of the revealed and the hidden: Georgian Jewry was always connected to the world of Kabbalah and esoteric teaching. Rabbi Yirmiyahu combined in his sermons kabbalistic ideas from the school of the Ari and the Rashash, but always took care to bring them down to the practical level of everyday life.
The importance of the community: his teaching emphasizes that no person can serve God alone. The community (kahal) is the body in which the Divine Presence dwells. Therefore, the struggle for the synagogues in 1924 was not only about buildings, but about the ability of the Divine Presence to dwell among Israel.[1]
Honoring the fathers: Rabbi Yirmiyahu regarded honoring the tradition of the fathers as a supreme value. He used to mention his father's work in Kutaisi as an example of self-sacrifice to which every Jew should aspire.[1]
Summary and Conclusions: A Legacy of Resilience and Hope
Rabbi Yirmiyahu Khakhiashvili was a critical link in the golden chain of the sages of Georgia. His work and teaching draw directly on the historical struggles of his father, Chacham Chaim, in the Kutaisi of the early twentieth century.[1]
The central insights that emerge from this survey are:
Rabbinic leadership in Georgian Jewry was characterized by a rare combination of halakhic authority and public activism, as can be seen in the struggle to return the synagogues in 1924.[1]
The bond with the Land of Israel was a powerful motive that prevailed even over the fear of long imprisonment and government persecution.[1]
Rabbi Yirmiyahu succeeded in carrying the spirit of devotion of Kutaisi into the modern reality of the State of Israel, while carefully preserving custom and tradition.
The legacy of Rabbi Yirmiyahu Khakhiashvili continues to resonate in Georgian communities in Israel and around the world. His figure serves as a reminder that true leadership is tested in the hardest hours, and that the power of Torah and faith can overcome harsh decrees and lead the public to a safe spiritual and physical shore. The work of his father, who served his community faithfully for twenty-four years and survived harsh ordeals of imprisonment, was Rabbi Yirmiyahu's moral and Torah compass throughout his path.[1] The building of synagogues, the preservation of customs and the longing for Zion are the three pillars on which his teaching stands, and it is they that ensured the survival of Georgian Jewry as a lively and believing community in the generations to come as well.
